Federal, state and local public health authorities have implemented response measures, including:

  • Epidemiological investigation of the confirmed human cases and their animal exposures.
  • Monitoring close contacts of the confirmed cases for signs and symptoms compatible with influenza.
  • Monitoring of people exposed to infected dairy cattle or contaminated environments.
  • Testing of symptomatic exposed persons for influenza, including influenza A(H5).
  • Enhanced surveillance to detect human infections with novel influenza A viruses.
  • Provision of information to potentially exposed workers on symptoms, testing and measures to reduce exposure.
  • Promotion and provision of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) for people exposed to infected animals or contaminated environments.
  • Continued virological characterization and sequencing of viruses detected in human and animal cases.
  • Coordination between public health and animal health authorities as part of the investigation.

US-CDC recommends monitoring people exposed to birds or other animals suspected or confirmed to be infected with avian influenza A viruses for signs and symptoms for up to 10 days after their last exposure. People who develop respiratory symptoms and/or conjunctivitis following such exposure should be tested for influenza.

WHO guidance similarly recommends identification and monitoring of at-risk groups, enhanced surveillance among occupationally exposed populations, appropriate clinical management and measures to reduce exposure to infected animals and contaminated environments.

These included one fatal case, the first reported death following exposure to infected dairy cattle or a related contaminated environment. All three cases were adults who worked on dairy cattle farms in Yakima County, Washington State, where the highly pathogenic (in animals) avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus had recently been detected in dairy cattle. Investigations and monitoring of exposed people and close contacts are ongoing. Based on information available to date, there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission. In accordance with the IHR (2005), any human infection caused by a new influenza A virus subtype is considered a potentially significant public health event and is subject to mandatory notification to WHO. Based on the information currently available on this and previous cases, WHO assesses the risk to the general population posed by A(H5N1) viruses as low. WHO continues to closely monitor these viruses and the global epidemiological situation.", "PublicationDateAndTime": "2026-11-24T19:00:00Z", "TitleSuffix": "", "UseOverrideTitle": true, "Title": "Influenza A(H5N1) - United States of America", "Epidemiology": "

Animal influenza viruses typically circulate within animal populations, but some have the potential to infect humans. Human infections are predominantly acquired through direct contact with infected animals or exposure to contaminated environments. Based on their original host species, influenza A viruses may be categorized as avian influenza viruses, swine influenza viruses, and other animal-origin influenza viruses.

Human infection with avian influenza viruses may result in a spectrum of illness, ranging from mild conjunctivitis and/or upper respiratory tract symptoms to severe, life-threatening conditions. Clinical manifestations may include conjunctivitis, respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, and less commonly neurological complications such as encephalitis and encephalopathy. In some cases, asymptomatic infections with the virus have been reported in individuals with known exposure to infected animals and environments.

A definitive diagnosis of human avian influenza infection requires laboratory confirmation. WHO regularly updates its technical guidance on the detection of zoonotic influenza, utilizing molecular diagnostic methods such as RT-PCR. Clinical evidence indicates that certain antiviral agents, particularly neuraminidase inhibitors (e.g., oseltamivir, zanamivir), have been shown to shorten the duration of viral replication and improve patient outcomes in some cases. When indicated, antiviral treatment should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset.

Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5) viruses belonging to H5 haemagglutinin clade 2.3.4.4b are widely circulating in wild birds and poultry and have also been detected in mammals, including dairy cattle in North America.

This event does not change current WHO recommendations on public health measures and surveillance for influenza.

Given the continuing circulation of avian influenza viruses in poultry, wild birds and some wild and domestic mammals, people should avoid unprotected contact with sick or dead animals and with environments potentially contaminated by infected animals.
